table.text: Five hundred and twenty-nine participants completed an online survey in which they provided the minimum amount of monetary compensation it would require to complete ten separate hypothetical scenarios, with the option to refuse any task.

For example, Tetlock and colleagues (2000) found that when participants were asked to consider monetary trade-offs for sacred values, they frequently displayed strong moral reactions and rejected the proposed exchange.
table.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Tetlock and colleagues (2000)</ref> found that when participants were asked to consider monetary trade-offs for sacred values, they frequently displayed strong moral reactions and rejected the proposed exchange.

table.text: Five hundred and thirty-three participants completed an online survey from March-June 2026.

Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling approach through the authors' personal and professional social networks, including social media, family and community networks, and online groups.
Subjects were asked to identify only if they were male, female or other.
Four subjects were removed due to failure to follow instructions.
Participants were instructed to input the amount of money they would require to complete ten hypothetical tasks.
Participants were instructed to respond with "no amount of money" if the task was something they would not do for any price.
Input values ranged from $0 to $1,000,000,000; participants were informed that responses over $1 billion dollars would be viewed the same as "no amount of money".
Four respondents provided answers that were clearly jokes with no recoverable monetary values; these participants were removed from all analyses.

We further found that the highest refusal rates among participants were observed almost exclusively in tasks that were permanent or irreversible, consistent with previous research on sacred values and taboo trade-offs (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Five hundred and twenty-nine participants completed an online survey in which they provided the minimum amount of monetary compensation it would require to complete ten separate hypothetical scenarios, with the option to refuse any task.

> For example, Tetlock and colleagues (2000) found that when participants were asked to consider monetary trade-offs for sacred values, they frequently displayed strong moral reactions and rejected the proposed exchange.

> Five hundred and thirty-three participants completed an online survey from March-June 2026.

> Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling approach through the authors' personal and professional social networks, including social media, family and community networks, and online groups.

> Subjects were asked to identify only if they were male, female or other.

> Four subjects were removed due to failure to follow instructions.

> Participants were instructed to input the amount of money they would require to complete ten hypothetical tasks.

> Participants were instructed to respond with "no amount of money" if the task was something they would not do for any price.

> Input values ranged from $0 to $1,000,000,000; participants were informed that responses over $1 billion dollars would be viewed the same as "no amount of money".

> Four respondents provided answers that were clearly jokes with no recoverable monetary values; these participants were removed from all analyses.

> We further found that the highest refusal rates among participants were observed almost exclusively in tasks that were permanent or irreversible, consistent with previous research on sacred values and taboo trade-offs (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).

> Last, participants were recruited using a voluntary online convenience sample, and other than gender, no demographic information was collected, thus limiting the generalizability of the findings.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .178", Sentence = "Interestingly, the highest refusal task overall, becoming 10 years older, showed no significant gender difference (74.9% vs 69.2%; p = .178)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Money is a universal measure of value that influences most decisions.
For centuries, humans have used it to exchange goods and experiences.
Research in psychology and behavioral economics, however, shows that there may be limits to what individuals are willing to exchange for money.
This study examined the monetary values people assign to personal experiences, and whether willingness to engage in monetary valuation differs between males and females.

Five hundred and twenty-nine participants completed an online survey in which they provided the minimum amount of monetary compensation it would require to complete ten separate hypothetical scenarios, with the option to refuse any task.
The hypothetical tasks ranged from temporary restrictions and social isolation to public disclosure, loss of memories and permanent identity changes.

Based on the results from previous economic decision-making studies, we hypothesized that females would refuse to price tasks more than males and that males would request higher compensation for priced tasks.
We also hypothesized that permanent or identity-altering tasks would result in higher refusal rates than temporary ones in both genders.
Whether resistance to monetary valuation is a consistent individual tendency was also examined.
Our results showed that participants who refused to price one hypothetical task were more likely to refuse other tasks.
While no gender differences were observed for any task regarding the monetary value requested, females refused significantly more tasks than males (4.43 vs.
Refusal rates were highest for permanent or identity-altering tasks and lowest for temporary tasks.
Lastly, refusal rates for loss of digital pictures/videos were nearly identical to losing contact with friends and family.
Together, these findings suggest that monetary valuation involves two separate decisions: whether or not to assign a monetary value and, if so, how much to request.
Individuals differ consistently in their willingness to engage in monetary valuation, and gender influences the decision to engage rather than with the amount requested.
People assign monetary values to things every day.

The price an individual is willing to pay for a new car, the salary requested for a particular job, or the proposed budget for a family vacation are all decisions that have an inherent financial valuation.
However, deciding on a particular price for ending all contact with a best friend or forever discontinuing a favorite hobby is more challenging.
For many individuals, assigning a monetary value to certain meaningful aspects of life is not only difficult, but feels morally inappropriate (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).

text.text: Importantly, this suggests that monetary valuation may involve an initial decision as to whether to engage prior to assigning a monetary amount.

Previous research has focused on the central factors that influence whether individuals are willing to assign a monetary value to certain outcomes or experiences. Fiske and Tetlock (1997) describe a concept known as "taboo trade-offs", which occurs when people are asked to provide a monetary value to something meaningful that the person believes should not be bought or sold.
text.formatted: Previous research has focused on the central factors that influence whether individuals are willing to assign a monetary value to certain outcomes or experiences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Fiske and Tetlock (1997)</ref> describe a concept known as "taboo trade-offs", which occurs when people are asked to provide a monetary value to something meaningful that the person believes should not be bought or sold.

text.text: The researchers assert that certain social rules are associated with specific relationship domains.
For example, financial decisions are usually based on economic reasoning, whereas decisions involving interpersonal relationships are influenced by social and moral beliefs.
When people are asked to assign a price to certain relationships or experiences, it is perceived as a violation of these principles.

Therefore, certain scenarios may be resistant to monetary valuation because assigning a price elicits moral outrage as opposed to hesitation about identifying an appropriate amount (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997). Tetlock (2003) extended this work to include sacred values-beliefs or relationships that are so important that people believe they should not be exchanged for money.

text.text: The Sacred Value Protection Model states that when people are asked to establish a price for a sacred value, they may refuse due to the belief that the value should not be measured in monetary terms.

While many of the scenarios proposed in the current study would not traditionally be considered sacred values, Tetlock's research suggests that individuals may resist valuation whenever they feel some meaningful aspect of life falls outside the range of economic exchange (Tetlock, 2003).

text.text: Previous research supports the Sacred Value Protection Model.

For example, Tetlock and colleagues (2000) found that when participants were asked to consider monetary trade-offs for sacred values, they frequently displayed strong moral reactions and rejected the proposed exchange.

text.text: Moreover, human neuroimaging studies by Berns et al. (2012) showed that participants' refusal to assign a monetary value to a sacred belief were associated with increased brain activity in regions implicated in moral judgment and rule retrieval, and not regions typically involved in evaluating costs and benefits.

(2012)</ref> showed that participants' refusal to assign a monetary value to a sacred belief were associated with increased brain activity in regions implicated in moral judgment and rule retrieval, and not regions typically involved in evaluating costs and benefits.

text.text: These protected values were highly stable over time, with over 96% showing no change at a 6-14-month follow-up (Berns et al., 2012).

text.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that refusing to assign a price to a sacred value is a unique reaction that is distinct from assigning an extremely high monetary value.

While the majority of previous research has focused on the resistance to valuation and the types of scenarios frequently rejected, much less attention has been given to how or if participant characteristics influence the decision-making process.

Specifically, do individuals differ in their willingness to place monetary values on meaningful aspects of life, and is the individuals' tendency to reject monetary trade-offs consistent across different types of scenarios?

If people who refuse to identify a price on one type of experience are also likely to refuse other types of experiences, then resistance to monetary valuation may be a relatively stable individual characteristic rather than a series of unrelated decisions.

Examination of the consistency in decision making is important as previous research suggests that the line between the values an individual believes are priceless and those they are willing to monetize is not completely fixed but rather is quite plastic.

For example, McGraw et al. (2003) reported that individuals were more likely to accept certain trade-offs when they perceived those trade-offs as inevitable, tragic, or routine, in contrast to when they voluntarily priced an exchange, suggesting how a situation is presented can influence whether people are willing to assign a monetary value.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">McGraw et al. (2003)</ref> reported that individuals were more likely to accept certain trade-offs when they perceived those trade-offs as inevitable, tragic, or routine, in contrast to when they voluntarily priced an exchange, suggesting how a situation is presented can influence whether people are willing to assign a monetary value.

text.text: Therefore, if situations can influence a person's willingness to identify a monetary value for an experience or object, then individuals may also show differences in their willingness to engage in the process (McGraw et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Therefore, if situations can influence a person's willingness to identify a monetary value for an experience or object, then individuals may also show differences in their willingness to engage in the process <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(McGraw et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This concept is called "commodification willingness" and is defined as a person's general tendency to engage in monetary valuation of meaningful experiences.
If commodification willingness is consistent across different scenarios, it may be a primary factor that influences how people make decisions regarding valuation.
An area of interest that is relatively unexplored is whether gender differences exist in valuation behavior.
Economic decision-making studies report that males and females display differences in their willingness to participate in situations that appear competitive or involve monetary incentives.

For example, Niederle and Vesterlund (2007) found that men and women performed similarly on a math computation task, yet men were almost twice as likely to choose a competitive performance-based payment option.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Niederle and Vesterlund (2007)</ref> found that men and women performed similarly on a math computation task, yet men were almost twice as likely to choose a competitive performance-based payment option.

text.text: The authors concluded that this difference between men and women was likely driven by male overconfidence and preference for competition as opposed to believing they were superior in ability.
These findings suggest that men and women may differ not only in economic decision making, but also in their willingness to engage in monetary valuation (Niederle & Vesterlund, 2007).
text.formatted: These findings suggest that men and women may differ not only in economic decision making, but also in their willingness to engage in monetary valuation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Niederle & Vesterlund, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: If gender differences do exist in valuation tasks, an important question is where they emerge in the decision-making process.
Prior to assigning a monetary value to an experience, individuals must first decide whether they are willing to evaluate the experience monetarily.
Next, a decision regarding the amount of compensation required is made.
Therefore, gender differences may exist in the decision to engage in monetary valuation, in the amount assigned, or both.

Decades of research on taboo trade-offs and sacred values have primarily focused on valuation responses in males, without considering potential gender differences in these two stages of decision making (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003; Berns et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Decades of research on taboo trade-offs and sacred values have primarily focused on valuation responses in males, without considering potential gender differences in these two stages of decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fiske & Tetlock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Tetlock, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Berns et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The current study addressed this gap in the literature by examining commodification willingness in a sample of 529 participants.
Males and females responded to ten hypothetical scenarios involving personal sacrifices and were given the option to either provide a monetary value or refuse valuation.
The scenarios ranged from temporary discomfort and public disclosure to social isolation, loss of personal memories, and permanent changes in identity.

The study further investigated whether refusal behavior is consistent across different scenarios, suggesting a stable individual tendency, and if there are gender differences in the willingness to engage in monetary valuation.
This study also assessed whether certain types of sacrifices are more resistant to valuation than others.

Based on previous research on economic decision making and taboo trade-offs, we hypothesized that refusal behavior would be consistent across scenarios, that females would display reduced willingness to engage in monetary valuation, and that males would assign higher monetary values than females overall.
We also hypothesized that permanent or identity-altering scenarios would produce higher refusal rates than temporary scenarios, regardless of gender.
Five hundred and thirty-three participants completed an online survey from March-June 2026.

Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling approach through the authors' personal and professional social networks, including social media, family and community networks, and online groups.
The survey was completed anonymously, and no personal identification information was collected.
Subjects were asked to identify only if they were male, female or other.
As no physiological samples were obtained to ascertain biological sex, the term "gender", defined here as the sex a person identifies with, was used.
Overall, 275 females (52.0%), 247 males (46.7%), and 7 who identified as "other" or preferred not to report (1.3%) participated in this study.
The seven participants in the latter category were included in all analyses except male/female comparisons.
Four subjects were removed due to failure to follow instructions.
Participants were instructed to input the amount of money they would require to complete ten hypothetical tasks.
Participants were instructed to respond with "no amount of money" if the task was something they would not do for any price.
Input values ranged from $0 to $1,000,000,000; participants were informed that responses over $1 billion dollars would be viewed the same as "no amount of money".
Each task was independent of the others.
The ten hypothetical scenarios were: 1.
Give up your phone and all personal technology for one full year.
Move far away and not see your closest friends or family for two years.
You cannot talk/communicate to said friends and family for the duration of the time away.
Let your entire search history be shown publicly (to everyone you know).
Have every text message you've ever sent be read out loud to a group of people (friends/family).
Spend 60 days completely alone in a room with no internet, phone, or outside contact.
(Still fed/living conditions) 6.
Give up all online/social entertainment (video games, television, social media, YouTube, etc.) for one year.
Lose all your saved photos/videos permanently.
Speak in front of 1,000 people about your biggest mistake.
Give up your favorite hobby or activity forever.
Immediately become 10 years older than you are now.
All responses were converted to standard numbers.
Responses over $1,000,000,000, as stated in the survey's instructions, were treated as a refusal to assign a monetary value.
Responses in which participants indicated they would perform the task for free were converted to $0.
Four respondents provided answers that were clearly jokes with no recoverable monetary values; these participants were removed from all analyses.
The number of tasks in which the participant refused to assign a monetary value was quantified for each person.
As the dollar amounts varied greatly for tasks ($0 to $1,000,000,000), mean values were not representative and therefore the median was used as the measure of central tendency.
Responses of $0 were included in the monetary analyses.
Responses were separated by gender; tasks were categorized as permanent (involved an irreversible loss or change of state) or non-permanent (temporary event even if it had lasting consequences).
Chi-Square tests of independence were used to compare refusal rates between males and females for each of the ten scenarios; p < .05 was considered significant.
text.formatted: Chi-Square tests of independence were used to compare refusal rates between males and females for each of the ten scenarios; p < .05 was considered significant.

text.text: Bonferroni correction was applied to maintain the type 1 error rate across the ten comparisons (adjusted α = .005).
Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test.
Because the values were heavily skewed, the nonparametric Mann Whitney U test (MWU), which does not assume a normal distribution, was used to compare median monetary values between males and females.
Effect sizes are shown as rank-biserial correlations (r), with .10 (small), .30 (medium), and .50 (large) effects, respectively.

To assess whether refusal was a consistent response within individuals (i.e., if people who refuse one task also tend to refuse other related and unrelated tasks), phi coefficients were calculated for the 45 pairs of tasks.
Each participant was coded as 1 for refusing a task and 0 for providing a monetary value.
A correlation across all participants was calculated to determine the relatedness of the two binary variables.
Chi-square tests were used to calculate p-values, and a Bonferroni correction was applied to the 45 comparisons (adjusted α = .0011).
Willingness to engage in monetization was assessed by quantifying the number of tasks (out of 10) each participant assigned a monetary value.
Gender differences in the average number of monetized tasks was assessed using an independent-samples t-test.
Mean ± SD values are reported for each gender, and Cohen's d was used to determine effect size.
To assess whether the overall pattern of association between tasks was similar across genders, correlation matrices were created for all participants (combined and separately for females and males).
The 45 female and male phi coefficients were then compared using Pearson's correlation (r) to assess the similarity between the two matrices.
Finally, the number of task pairs that differed in statistical significance after Bonferroni correction was quantified.
We first examined refusal rates for permanent versus temporary tasks.
Overall, refusal rates ranged from 10.0% (give up online entertainment for one year) to 72.0% (become ten years older) (Table 1).
text.formatted: Overall, refusal rates ranged from 10.0% (give up online entertainment for one year) to 72.0% (become ten years older) (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The three tasks with the highest refusal rates were permanent, while the three tasks with the lowest refusal rates were temporary.
In total, 53.7% of participants refused to relinquish all photos/videos forever, 55.2% refused to permanently give up their favorite hobby, and 72.0% refused to age 10 years.
In contrast, the three tasks with the lowest refusal rate were all temporary (give up entertainment, 10.0%; public speaking, 14.2%; no electronics, 18.0%).
Refusal rates were almost identical for refusing to lose all photos/videos forever (53.7%) and moving away from friends/family for 2 years (53.5%).

For participants who named a price, the median values across all ten scenarios ranged from $50,000 for speaking in front of 1,000 people about their biggest mistake to $5,000,000 for becoming 10 years older (Table 1).
text.formatted: For participants who named a price, the median values across all ten scenarios ranged from $50,000 for speaking in front of 1,000 people about their biggest mistake to $5,000,000 for becoming 10 years older (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The three tasks with the highest median monetary values were all permanent scenarios.
Specifically, the median amount requested was $1,000,000 to lose all photos/videos forever, $1,000,000 to permanently give up a favorite hobby, and $5,000,000 to become ten years older (Table 1).
text.formatted: Specifically, the median amount requested was $1,000,000 to lose all photos/videos forever, $1,000,000 to permanently give up a favorite hobby, and $5,000,000 to become ten years older (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Of these three, giving up a favorite hobby forever had the smallest range of monetary values.
To assess whether resistance to monetary valuation is a consistent tendency within an individual, phi correlations were calculated for all 45 pairs of tasks.
Most correlations were positive: 43 of the 45 pairs, and 34 of the 45 pairs were significant (α = .0011).
The phi correlation matrices show the pattern of associations between refusal responses across tasks (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The phi correlation matrices show the pattern of associations between refusal responses across tasks (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: These analyses suggest that participants who refused one task were more likely to refuse other tasks.
The strongest correlation was between the two digital sacrifice tasks (φ = .40); however, clustering was not limited to similar scenarios.

For example, a significant correlation was also noted between "move away 2 yrs" and "lose all photos/videos" (φ = .37) and giving up online entertainment and speaking in front of 1,000 people (φ = .33) despite the tasks being seemingly unrelated.
Taken together, the data suggests the tendency to resist monetary valuation as a whole is such that individuals who refuse to put a value on a single task are more likely to refuse others.
This pattern was observed across both related and unrelated scenarios.
We next compared the 45 phi correlations between females and males.
The overall patterns of associations were similar (Pearson r = .72).
Seven of the 10 strongest correlations were the same for both genders.
However, the patterns were not identical, and 7 of the 45 task pairs (16%) showed statistically significant associations for one gender but not the other.

Two task pairs showed the clearest gender differences: search history × giving up online entertainment and search history × speaking to 1,000 people were related for females (φ ≈ .21-.24) but not for males (φ ≈ .05-.07) (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Two task pairs showed the clearest gender differences: search history × giving up online entertainment and search history × speaking to 1,000 people were related for females (φ ≈ .21-.24) but not for males (φ ≈ .05-.07) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Females Refuse More, Task by Task Gender differences in refusal rates across all ten tasks are shown in Figure 2.
text.formatted: Females Refuse More, Task by Task Gender differences in refusal rates across all ten tasks are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Females refused more often than males in 7 of the 10 tasks, with significant gender differences in 4 of the 10 tasks.
The largest gender difference in refusal rate (34.6%) was in the task "lose photos/videos" (69.8% females vs 35.2% males; p < .001).
text.formatted: The largest gender difference in refusal rate (34.6%) was in the task "lose photos/videos" (69.8% females vs 35.2% males; p < .001).

text.text: Significantly higher refusal rates were observed for females in 60 days alone (45.1% females vs 20.6% males; p < .001), moving away for two years (64.7% females vs 40.9% males; p < .001), and giving up electronics for a year (22.9% females vs 12.1% ; p = .002).
text.formatted: Significantly higher refusal rates were observed for females in 60 days alone (45.1% females vs 20.6% males; p < .001), moving away for two years (64.7% females vs 40.9% males; p < .001), and giving up electronics for a year (22.9% females vs 12.1% ; p = .002).

text.text: Two other tasks, speaking in front of 1,000 people (p = .032) and giving up a favorite hobby (p = .019), showed gender differences, but were not significant.
Interestingly, the highest refusal task overall, becoming 10 years older, showed no significant gender difference (74.9% vs 69.2%; p = .178).
We next examined whether males and females who chose to price a task requested different amounts of money.
Overall, there were no significant gender differences in the amounts requested for any of the 10 tasks (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Overall, there were no significant gender differences in the amounts requested for any of the 10 tasks (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The median amounts for females and males, along with the MWU test results and effect sizes, are shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.
text.formatted: The median amounts for females and males, along with the MWU test results and effect sizes, are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> and Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: For public speaking, females asked for a higher median amount than males (p = .021), but this difference was not significant.
To test whether females were more likely to refuse to assign a monetary value than males, we compared the average number of tasks each gender chose to price.
Males priced an average of 6.83 out of 10 tasks (SD = 2.09), compared with 5.57 for females (SD = 2.28) (p < .001; Cohen's d = 0.56) (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Males priced an average of 6.83 out of 10 tasks (SD = 2.09), compared with 5.57 for females (SD = 2.28) (p < .001; Cohen's d = 0.56) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Overall, 55.9% of males and 31.3% of females priced 7 or more (χ² = 32.14, p < .001; φ = .248) (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Overall, 55.9% of males and 31.3% of females priced 7 or more (χ² = 32.14, p < .001; φ = .248) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: These results suggest that the main gender difference is primarily in regards to opting out of monetization rather than pricing differently.
The present study examined whether individuals differ in their willingness to assign monetary values to meaningful experiences across a range of scenarios.
It also assessed whether gender differences exist in monetization and refusal behavior, as well as in valuation amount.
The data show that refusal behavior was consistent across scenarios, such that individuals who refuse valuation on one task were more likely to resist monetization in general.
This result suggests that willingness to engage in monetary valuation is a strong individual tendency and not a series of unrelated choices.

We further found that the highest refusal rates among participants were observed almost exclusively in tasks that were permanent or irreversible, consistent with previous research on sacred values and taboo trade-offs (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).
text.formatted: We further found that the highest refusal rates among participants were observed almost exclusively in tasks that were permanent or irreversible, consistent with previous research on sacred values and taboo trade-offs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fiske & Tetlock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Tetlock, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Gender differences were mainly observed in the participants' willingness to engage in monetary valuation instead of the values they assigned.
Females displayed higher refusal rates for valuation of the tasks and monetized fewer tasks compared to males.
For the tasks that participants did choose to monetize, however, there were no significant gender differences in the amounts requested.
Females asked for more money for public speaking than males, but this difference was not significant.
Finally, refusal rates for the permanent loss of all digital pictures and videos were nearly identical to losing contact with friends and family for two years.
The current results regarding refusal behavior are consistent with previous research on taboo trade-offs and sacred values.

According to this line of research, individuals are unwilling to monetize certain relationships or values because it violates the social and moral standards associated with those domains (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).
text.formatted: According to this line of research, individuals are unwilling to monetize certain relationships or values because it violates the social and moral standards associated with those domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fiske & Tetlock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Tetlock, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that refusing to assign a monetary value to certain scenarios is not only about the type of experience being evaluated, but also about the individual making that decision.
Participants who refused to put a price on one task were more likely to refuse other tasks, including unrelated ones.
This observed pattern was in 34 of the 45 task pairs.
Furthermore, many of the strongest relationships were observed between dissimilar types of tasks.
These results suggest that willingness to engage in monetization of meaningful experiences is a consistent individual tendency across different domains.
Interestingly, as stated above, the relationships between tasks were not restricted to similar scenarios.

While participants who refused one technology-related experience frequently refused others in the same category, there were many other significant associations across distinct and unrelated domains including personal relationships, memories, privacy, and hobbies.

One interesting finding was that participants displayed similar refusal rates to giving up all personal technology for one year and spending 60 days in complete isolation, suggesting that participants found these two very different experiences similarly resistant to monetization.
Instead of considering each scenario independently, some participants seemed to be very willing to commodify meaningful experiences, whereas others who refused did not.

Future studies should focus on whether this is a stable individual difference in commodification willingness and the types of factors influencing this decision behavior, such as age and level of education.
Our findings also identified where gender differences exist in the monetary valuation process.
Females refused to assign monetary values significantly more often than males in four of the ten scenarios, and on average, assigned prices to a lower number of tasks.
In contrast, males priced more tasks on average than females.
This suggests that the main gender difference was in whether participants chose to assign a monetary value, rather than in how much money they requested once they chose to monetize.

This finding is consistent with previous research showing that males and females display differences in their willingness to enter into environments that are perceived as competitive or economic, even when performance levels are similar (Niederle & Vesterlund, 2007).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with previous research showing that males and females display differences in their willingness to enter into environments that are perceived as competitive or economic, even when performance levels are similar <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Niederle & Vesterlund, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Before assigning a price to a meaningful experience, an initial decision must be made as to whether or not to participate in the valuation process.
Our results suggest that females are less likely to engage in this initial step.
Once the decision is made to monetize an experience, no gender differences in monetary amounts were noted across the ten tasks.
This is consistent with previous research on taboo trade-offs in which the idea of monetizing certain aspects of life feels morally inappropriate (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous research on taboo trade-offs in which the idea of monetizing certain aspects of life feels morally inappropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fiske & Tetlock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Tetlock, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The gender differences observed here are mainly in regards to the willingness to engage in monetization rather than differences in the actual valuation of meaningful experiences.
Females who priced the public speaking task requested a higher amount than males, but this difference was not significant.

Public speaking differs from the other scenarios in the study because it involves being evaluated by others and performing in front of an audience as opposed to giving up something meaningful or experiencing a permanent loss.
There was a clear pattern in the scenarios which were the most and least resistant to monetary valuation.
Specifically, the three scenarios with the highest rates of refusal all involved permanent or irreversible losses and the three lowest refusals involved temporary disruptions.

These results are consistent with previous research on sacred values suggesting that some values are inherently resistant to monetization because they are viewed as non-negotiable or morally offensive (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003).
text.formatted: These results are consistent with previous research on sacred values suggesting that some values are inherently resistant to monetization because they are viewed as non-negotiable or morally offensive <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fiske & Tetlock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Tetlock, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, permanence and irreversibility may be characteristics of an experience that increase the likelihood of refusing monetary valuation, and this pattern was evident in both males and females.
This present study revealed an interesting finding regarding stored digital photos and videos.
Participants refused to assign monetary values to permanently deleting their photos at almost the same rate as they refused to cut off all contact with loved ones for two years.
While these experiences may seem distinct, digital photos are becoming a modern collection of autobiographical and social memories.

This concept is consistent with previous research showing that digital property, including photos, videos, social media profiles, and email/text messages, have become part of an individual's extended personal identity in the digital age (Belk, 2013 , Honarvar & Sepehrinia, 2025).
text.formatted: This concept is consistent with previous research showing that digital property, including photos, videos, social media profiles, and email/text messages, have become part of an individual's extended personal identity in the digital age <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Belk, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">, Honarvar & Sepehrinia, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is likely that participants treated the permanent loss of digital memories as a major sacrifice they were not willing to monetize.
It would be interesting to assess in future studies if attachment to digital property differs across generations and cultures.
The present findings have important implications for research on taboo trade-offs and moral decision making.

Consistent with previous research on sacred values and taboo trade-offs, the findings here suggest that some experiences are considered inappropriate to monetize (Fiske & Tetlock, 1997; Tetlock, 2003; Atran & Ginges, 2012).
text.formatted: Consistent with previous research on sacred values and taboo trade-offs, the findings here suggest that some experiences are considered inappropriate to monetize <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Fiske & Tetlock, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Tetlock, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Atran & Ginges, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Prior studies have primarily focused on determining what types of experiences are resistant to monetization (Atran & Ginges, 2012).
text.formatted: Prior studies have primarily focused on determining what types of experiences are resistant to monetization <ref type="bibr">(Atran & Ginges, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The current study extends this literature by highlighting the characteristics of the individuals making the decisions as an important factor.

Furthermore, our work suggests that monetary valuation is not a single decision but is actually a two-step process that involves the initial decision of whether to assign a monetary value and then determining the amount to request.

Because refusal behavior clustered within individuals across both related and unrelated scenarios, future studies should focus on why some individuals consistently reject monetary valuation while others readily engage in this type of exchange.

These findings suggest that commodification willingness may be a meaningful individual difference that impacts how a person responds when asked to assign monetary values to important relationships and life experiences.
This research will provide greater insight into how people make economic decisions when they involve sacred values, close relationships, and moral beliefs.
The current results have important implications for future research on related topics.
Specifically, research on taboo trade-offs should differentiate between two separate responses: the decision to assign a monetary value and the amount requested.
Moreover, instead of considering a refusal response as missing data, it should be viewed as a meaningful decision.

Our findings also suggest that the individual differences in the choice to engage in monetary valuation are much larger than in the amount of compensation requested once people have decided to participate.
Several limitations of the current study should be considered when interpreting the results.
First, the study relied on hypothetical scenarios instead of real financial incentives; therefore, participant responses may be different than their actual behavior.

Second, because many of the characteristics of the scenarios were different (i.e., permanent loss, personally meaningful, public evaluation), it is unknown which features affected the choice to refuse or assign a value.
Third, although the refusal behavior was very consistent across scenarios, the current study did not examine whether these effects would be stable across time.
Fourth, asking participants to either assign a monetary value or refuse may oversimplify the willingness of people to put a price on meaningful experiences.
Last, participants were recruited using a voluntary online convenience sample, and other than gender, no demographic information was collected, thus limiting the generalizability of the findings.
Future studies may want to collect additional data, including age, level of education, and socioeconomic status.

In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that assigning monetary values to meaningful experiences involves two different decisions: whether to participate in monetary valuation, and if so, how much compensation is required.

The current findings suggest that people differ in their willingness to put a price on meaningful experiences, and that gender differences occur mainly in the decision to do so, rather than in the amount of money requested once participants choose to engage.

Taken together, these findings add to existing literature on taboo trade-offs by showing that understanding who chooses to monetize meaningful experiences may be just as important as understanding which experiences are valued.
